lesson.title: One Formula to Rule Every Power: Introducing the Power Rule
lesson.summary: The power rule says that the derivative of x raised to a whole number power n is n times x raised to the power n minus 1, and it can be proven directly from the limit definition using the binomial expansion.
lesson.body:
Among all the differentiation rules, the power rule is the one you will use most often, because so many functions in algebra and calculus are built from powers of x. The rule states that for a positive whole number n, the derivative of f(x) = x^n is f'(x) = n times x^(n-1). In words: bring the exponent down as a multiplying factor, then subtract one from the exponent. It looks almost too simple to be true, so it is worth proving carefully rather than just accepting it.

The proof relies on expanding (x+h)^n using the binomial theorem, but the pattern is already visible for small n. Take n = 3, so f(x) = x^3. Using the binomial expansion, (x+h)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3. Subtracting f(x) = x^3 leaves f(x+h) - f(x) = 3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3. Every remaining term has at least one factor of h, so dividing by h gives 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2, with no division problems since h has been fully factored out. Now take the limit as h approaches 0: the term 3xh goes to 0, and h^2 goes to 0, leaving only 3x^2. This matches the power rule prediction exactly, since n x^(n-1) with n = 3 gives 3x^(3-1) = 3x^2.

This same pattern holds for any positive whole number n: when you expand (x+h)^n, the first term is x^n, the second term is n x^(n-1) h, and every term after that carries at least two factors of h. Subtracting x^n and dividing by h leaves n x^(n-1) as the only term without a leftover factor of h, and every other term still has at least one h remaining, so it vanishes as h approaches 0. That is the general proof of the power rule for positive integer exponents, and it is the same mechanism you just watched play out concretely for n = 3.

For a numerical check, consider f(x) = x^5. The power rule gives f'(x) = 5x^4. At x = 2, this evaluates to 5 times 2^4, and since 2^4 = 16, the result is 5 times 16, which is 80. So the tangent line to y = x^5 at x = 2 has slope 80, meaning the function is increasing very steeply there, which makes sense given how quickly x^5 grows.

The power rule as proven here covers positive whole number exponents, which is enough to differentiate any polynomial once it is combined with the constant, sum, difference, and constant multiple rules. Later chapters extend the same formula, n x^(n-1), to negative whole number exponents and to fractional exponents, using slightly different arguments since the binomial expansion used above only applies cleanly to positive integer powers. The formula itself, however, stays exactly the same across all of these extensions, which is part of why the power rule is so remarkably useful.

It is also worth checking the rule against a case simple enough to verify by other means: n = 1, so f(x) = x. The power rule predicts f'(x) = 1 times x^0, and since x^0 = 1 for any nonzero x, this gives f'(x) = 1. That matches what you already know about the line y = x, whose slope is 1 everywhere, confirming the formula holds even at this smallest possible whole number exponent. Seeing the power rule agree with a fact you can check by pure geometry, alongside the algebraic proof above, is a good habit whenever you meet a new general formula: test it against a case you can verify independently before trusting it fully in more complicated settings.
